introFa: کتاب «The Muse» نوشته Jessie Burton یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Muse»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 5 Samantha Sheppard, “JCMS Spotlight: Q&A Black Caucus Co-Chairs Nsenga Burton and Mark Cunningham,” JCMS 60, no. 3 (Spring 2021): 5–8. Interview by Samantha Sheppard Spotlight: Q&A with Black Caucus Co-­ Chairs Nsenga Burton and Mark Cunningham Samantha Sheppard: What does it mean to study, write, and teach about Black film and media during this current cultural moment and political climate? Nsenga Burton and Mark Cunningham: Studying, writing, and teaching Black film means bringing awareness and attention to the work of Black film- makers and media makers, exposing people to films made by Black filmmak- ers that they would not necessarily see or be open to seeing previously. Even though the US social and political climate is soaked in anti-­Black racism, it has also exposed allies who are actually interested in learning about Black culture and Black cultural production and putting their power in Hollywood and media-­adjacent industries to work toward equity, inclusion, and creating social change. As scholars who are tasked with teaching content that may cause students to confront their biases and prejudices, this moment presents an opportunity to elevate Black film history, culture, and production in the classroom, canon, and the field of film and media studies—­which we’ve been trying to do for a long time. Teaching this material is already a challenge in many of the institutions in which Black scholars teach, but in this current moment, there appears to be at least a diverse body of people amenable to working with Black scholars and creators to elevate Black film, history, and culture and give them the weight they deserve in academia. Sheppard: Do you have any recommendations for colleges and learned societies like SCMS about how the unique circumstances of the pandemic and state-­sanctioned anti-­ Black violence are impacting Black scholars?

6 JCMS 60.3 • SPRING 2021 Burton and Cunningham: Our recommendation is to use classroom and societal spaces to have open and transparent dialogue about pressing issues like state-­sanctioned anti-­Black racism and violence. We have a robust Face- book page and welcome open and respectful dialogue about these issues. In addition, the Caucus offers insight and best practices on how to use what is happening in this moment in course content and classroom instruction. As for the climate, Black scholars have been working in often hostile and less than respectful climates for a very long time, so this challenge is not new to us. However, we now need to identify ways to accommodate this “newfound” interest in the study of Black film history, culture, and media production. This most recent attack on Black people in this country is part of a cycle, and we are under no impression that this “new” interest in our collective struggle and scholarly field will remain in perpetuity. While this particular moment is here, we encourage scholars to act on it and make the most of the opportuni- ties presented by departments and administrations to shed light on issues like inequity, anti-­Black racism, transphobia, and other concerns that can be and are readily discussed within the context of our field. Sheppard: What is exciting about the current landscape of Black media develop- ment, production, and access? Burton and Cunningham: It is probably easier to make a list of what is not exciting as opposed to the exciting opportunities in front of Black scholars and media makers today, because there are so many. 7 SHEPPARD • JCMS SPOTLIGHT: TSENGA BURTON AND MARK CUNNINGHAM seeing a lot of new Black-­owned or Black-­led production companies emerge, such as those helmed by Kenya Barris, Yara Shahidi, and Michael B. Jordan. Their emergence suggests that there will be more Black-­themed content in the cinematic landscape. We know, historically, there are not many Black people in positions of power in the traditional Hollywood film industry, but we are seeing more Black content put into development and the reprisal of canceled shows that featured Black casts, which help to showcase the Black talent that has always been available in the industry. We are also excited about the inclusion riders that are becoming status quo and the push to have more Black representation among agents, publicists, financiers, and other important members of media production. The great things that are happening in terms of opportunities for streaming, content creation, and distribution and even digital platform entities like Open Television (OTV) are exciting for Black creators, scholars, and the like. We are enjoying seeing Black documentaries and seeing Black folks move from web series to produc- tion deals in Hollywood, not to mention scholars whose work is becoming more and more a part of mainstream online and physical media spaces. We are also enjoying the number of emerging Black film festivals and cheering Black directors who have worked primarily in the indie world getting an opportunity to showcase their talents in Hollywood. Of course, the number of Black-­led, Black-­themed documentaries and Black literature being made into outstanding content is also inspiring. Sheppard: As co-chairs of the Black Caucus, what do you want to highlight about the Caucus’s initiatives, membership, or mission? Burton and Cunningham: The Black Caucus is a progressive caucus that is committed to ensuring Black scholars and filmmakers have a voice and influ- ence in SCMS. We are also a space to inform and encourage the exchange of ideas for the good of all caucus members. We are a safe space for discuss- ing issues around professional development, anti-­Black racism on college campuses, classroom management, pedagogical best practices, and any other issues of concern that our members might have. We also recognize that func- tioning in a pandemic causes additional stressors, particularly for members who are bearing the brunt of the pandemic in a myriad of ways, so we hope to be a space for addressing pandemic-­related concerns as well. Membership is open to people of African descent and allies who are part-­time or full-­time faculty, independent scholars, or researchers at an academic or research-­ based organization or institution. Please know that the focus of the Caucus is Black people and the global study of Black film, media, history, and cultural production. We will continue to bring forth opportunities to Black Caucus members in the form of job announcements, conferences, and funding opportunities. Currently, we are in discussions about creating initiatives that serve our members without adding to the unpaid labor Black scholars and researchers already experience. This interview has been edited for clarity.

8 JCMS 60.3 • SPRING 2021 Nsenga K. Burton, PhD, is co-director of Film and Media Management at Emory University. An expert on intersectionality and media, Dr. Burton is founder and editor-­in-­chief of The Burton Wire, an award-­winning news blog. Mark D. Cunningham, PhD, is an associate professor in Radio-­Television-­Film at Austin Community College in Austin, Texas. His research focuses include film, tele- vision, and media studies and Black popular culture.
